According to that report obtained by the Washington Post, supporters of the current president see January 6th, 2021, as the last opportunity to overturn the results of the presidential election. This sense of desperation and disappointment may lead to more incentive to become violent. Unlike previous post-election protests, the targets of the pro-Trump supporters are not necessarily the counter-protesters as they were previously, but rather, Congress itself is the target for January 6. The day before the riota stormed the Congress, an FBI office in Virginia also issued an explicit warning that extremists were preparing to travel to Washington to commit violence and quote, war, according to internal reports. The FBI report cited to an online post where the user declared the Trump supporters should go to Washington and get violent. The supporters said, quote, stop calling this a march or a rally or a protest. Go there ready for war. We get our president or we die. These threat warnings were not just hypothetical. By the night of January 6 attack, DC Police had already made six arrests in connection with the planned protests on charges of carrying weapons, ammunition, assault, assaulting police. This is all in public view. All of it. The truth is usually seen and rarely heard. Truth is truth whether denied or not. And leading up to the event, there were hundreds, hundreds of posts online showing that his supporters took this as a call to arms to attack the capital. And yet, in the face of all this, these credible warnings of serious, dangerous threats to our Capitol, when those thousands of people were standing in front of President Trump ready to take orders and attack, this is what he said. assumptions.text: The President of the United States holds sufficient influence over his supporters to shape their actions and intentions.
Public posts on social media platforms reflect genuine intent and planning, not hyperbole or exaggeration.
Law enforcement and intelligence agencies interpret online threats as actionable risks requiring intervention.
Supporters who referenced 'storming the Capitol' interpreted the language as authorization from Trump.
Trump’s rhetoric created a shared narrative among followers that the election was stolen and required forceful resistance.
Supporters believed they were acting under the direction or approval of the Commander-in-Chief.
The presence of detailed attack plans online indicates premeditated criminal behavior rather than idle discussion.
Monitoring online activity by political figures implies awareness of imminent danger.
Violent mobilization was facilitated by perceived legitimacy derived from top-down endorsement.
The use of military metaphors ('war', 'cavalry') reflects a collective psychological shift toward armed confrontation.
